Un lundi soir de mai, sept jeunes montré: On a Monday evening in May, seven young Montrealers gathered on the premises of La Converse. For most of them, it was the first time they had met. Without realizing it, they were about to forge bonds that would unite them forever. Some arrive almost an hour early, others rush in at the last minute. Once everyone is there, the young adults gather around the one who will be their mentor for the next few weeks. Raccoon, iced coffee always in hand, then kicks off the first “rapological” writing workshop, which will help everyone write their shared project, that of the Messagers Converse.
L’idée est simple, mais particulière : r: The idea is simple, but unusual: take the musical production of <l1>Kery James’s “Banlieusards”</l1> and remix it, updating it to suit today’s tastes and… Montréal’s. So it’s in a spirit of community and commitment that Terry Wouj, Kamilou, Youbee, SteinZ, Dreamkid, Snowside and Enomis are pooling their skills for the length of a rap track. The goal is to offer young Montrealers for whom rap is an integral part of their lives the chance to take part in a one-of-a-kind project.
Le morceau éponyme du rappeur Kery James: The eponymous track by rapper Kery James, who holds French and Haitian citizenship, often defines him as a “conscious rapper.” For many, the 45-year-old artist is one of the most important conscious rappers in France. That is partly because of the public and political issues he addresses, but also because of the problems he says France has suffered from over the past several decades.
Des sujets comme la pauvreté, la corrupt: Subjects like poverty, corruption, racism and Islamophobia run through what Kery James recounts. In “Banlieusards,” released in 2008, the author points a finger at the stigmatization experienced by young people in the French banlieues. With his words, the artist tries to restore their image, often tarnished in the mainstream media and public opinion.
À Montréal, ce sont des sujets similaire: In Montréal, similar issues – though not limited to these – concern the youth of neglected neighbourhoods. It is through the writing workshops Raccoon teaches the Messagers Converse that these concerns are addressed. Among them, the young people speak of precarity, poverty and the social isolation of certain communities. In their lyrics, the Messagers Converse talk about problems that affect them personally, but also society as a whole. Lines like “Poverty, what idiocy; it’s the leaders who control it” (Youbee) or “They label my people minority; gentrification of neighbourhoods is a priority” (Snowside) are proof of this and give concrete form to the hardships the authors live.
Mais les <em>Messagers Converse</em> évo: But the Messagers Converse also raise personal concerns. Like Kery James, through their project these young people nurture the hope that they themselves are not destined for a bleak life. Optimism and the prospect of a dignified life for themselves come through in the song’s lyrics, but also across the rapper’s entire body of work.
Reprendre ce classique du rap engagé et: Reworking this classic of conscious rap and applying it to the realities of young people and neighbourhoods in the Montréal metropolis is an editorial choice by La Converse, backed by the organizing team, and even deemed necessary by Raccoon thanks to his abilities as a lyricist in the context of this project with the youth.
L'œuvre de Kery James résonne aujourd’hu: Kery James’s work still resonates around the world today. Young people from neighbourhoods across the Francophonie feel called out by the French artist’s message, from the Paris banlieues to the streets of Saint-Michel, in Montréal. “Illegality is not a road to follow, because it’s a path with only two endings: death or prison,” are words echoed by Arris, a young teen who has previously confided in La Converse about the crime and violence affecting more and more youth in his neighbourhood.
C’est un groupe de sept artistes qui com: A group of seven artists makes up this year’s MC Converse edition. Among the participants are personalities as different as they are complementary, from all walks of life and with all kinds of stories from Montréal. “What matters to me is that the participants feel comfortable,” says Raccoon, speaking of his mentoring of the Messagers Converse. “The main thing is that they learn something. I wanted them to be part of a project they love, to come out of this experience with something to take with them.”
Issus des quatre coins de Montréal, les: Coming from all corners of Montréal, the Messagers Converse are all young people who have been marked by the routine, dreary life of their respective neighbourhoods. From Saint-Laurent to Saint-Michel, by way of Côte-des-Neiges and Villeray, everyday life in Montréal’s more disadvantaged neighbourhoods is experienced differently by each of the artists. Through their lines, their concerns have been given form and shared through the art of conscious rap.
Terry Wouj, de Port-au-Prince à Montréal: Terry Wouj, from Port-au-Prince to Montréal
Terry est un jeune aspirant artiste orig: Terry is a young aspiring artist from Haiti. He has been playing at rap on his own or with friends for a good four years, but it’s this year that he decided to officially dip his toe into the public world of Hip-Hop. Being a Messager Converse allowed the young Montréal-Nord resident to share his unique daily life by writing a very personal verse.
Un portrait de Terry Wouj. Photo: Rin Ea: A portrait of Terry Wouj. Photo: Rin Eadie
Arrivé à Montréal-Nord à l’âge de huit a: Arriving in Montréal-Nord at the age of eight, Terry took time to adapt to his new Montréal life. “In Haiti, everyone is Black. There’s less difference between the majority and the minority since it isn’t based on skin colour. When I got here, it was the opposite that shocked me,” he says of his identity. “I see and live problems no one would have in my home country. Things like racial profiling, for example, don’t exist in Haiti,” he continues in the same vein. Tying in with the lyrics of his verse, where he says, “I’m fed up with being underrepresented; where I’m from, the police are my ethnicity,” Terry points in particular to injustices linked to racism, much more present in certain parts of the city, like Montréal-Nord.
Pour comprendre les diverses références: To understand Terry’s various references to his culture of origin, Haitian culture, you have to look at his personal history. He talks a lot about what makes Montréal, its hoods and its culture. He of course mentions the melting pot of outside influences that came together to create a unique place on the island, but also the different people he comes across in local popular culture. “What pushes me forward is seeing the people around me and drawing inspiration from them. Especially in Montréal,” Terry confides.
Ceux qui l’ont motivé à se lancer dans l: Those who motivated him to get into music and to want to succeed are his own Hood Heroes, like Shreez, Tai TL or Citron Rose. “As a Haitian in Montréal, seeing my culture succeed here is a source of pride. It helped me feel more at home, less disoriented when I arrived. I feel like all Montrealers are close to me, just from the slang, for example.”
Une personnalité un peu timide et réserv: A somewhat shy and reserved personality like Kamilou’s – Kamille is her real name – can slip under the radar in a group. Quiet and discreet at first, Kamilou is completely transformed when the mic is in her hands. Her contribution to the Messagers Converse is very personal, addressing the world’s ills through her own personal struggles.
Un portrait de Kamilou. Photo: Rin Eadie: A portrait of Kamilou. Photo: Rin Eadie
Dans son couplet, elle évoque beaucoup l: In her verse, she talks a lot about the boys’ club that makes up the whole world, but particularly the rap scene. “Here, the Hip-Hop scene isn’t necessarily driven by women. There are some, but they don’t get the recognition that goes with the work they do,” she begins. “I pushed myself to rap in public because it could be a kind of inspiration for some, or a kind of pat on the back for others to start out as rappers.”
Qu’est-ce qui a inspiré Kamilou dans l’é: What inspired Kamilou in writing these lines? In part, it’s the special relationship she has with her mother. “My mother raised me alone all my life. She didn’t earn much, and we always lived in public housing. Yet I never lacked for anything. She inspired me a lot, she’s like my ‘Hood Hero,’” she says with a half-smile. Shy at first about sharing her story, Kamilou gains confidence when it comes to talking about the concerns that led her to pick up the mic. “Rap has also helped me psychologically.” Laughing, she even adds: “Writing songs is a lot cheaper than a psychologist, but it helps me enormously.”
Youbee et le maniement des mots: Youbee and his way with words
Younesse Benkhedda, alias Youbee, est un: Younesse Benkhedda, alias Youbee, is a young Montrealer who got into rap after discovering his love for words and the French language. Nimble with the pen, he finds in rap a way to escape and to share his vision of the world.
« Je me considère comme un rappeur engag: “I consider myself a conscious rapper. In life, I like to laugh, have a good time and not think too much about negative things. When I write, though, I see it as a way to convey a message. So it becomes important for me to write things that will touch people,” he explains.
Un portrait de Youbee. Photo: Rin Eadie: A portrait of Youbee. Photo: Rin Eadie
Âgé seulement de vingt ans, Youbee est d: Only twenty years old, Youbee is of Algerian origin. He is living his youth as an immigrant in Montréal, and shares his way of seeing what surrounds him through his words. His identity as an immigrant in the city makes him see the world differently.
La contribution de Youbee dans le projet: Youbee’s contribution to the MC Converse project is heavy with meaning. Some lines are political and clearly denounce the various shortcomings in his environment. Poverty, inequality, racism; his verse is deeply committed. Beyond the political references, what comes up often in his performance is his love for Montréal and his sense of belonging to it. Asked about his experience of the city, he says he doesn’t “attach [himself] to just one neighbourhood. I grew up in the Plateau and in Villeray, but I identify with the whole city. I’m always outside, always on the move, whether it’s in Rivière-Des-Prairies or Notre-Dame-de-Grâce.”
Ce « citoyen de Montréal » est animé par: This “citizen of Montréal” is driven by a community spirit. “What I like about the Messagers Converse concept – and about the world of rap in general – is that unifying tendency. In rap, everyone is equal, everyone shares their vision for others, everyone comes together around an art they’re passionate about. It’s that community aspect that drew me in and still fulfils me today,” he concludes.
La rage de briser le cycle et SteinZ: SteinZ and the rage to break the cycle
Issue du quartier Saint-Laurent dans le: From the Saint-Laurent neighbourhood in the north of Montréal, SteinZ is a 22-year-old rapper of Haitian and Gambian origin. For her, being a woman in a world dominated by a male presence like Hip-Hop is a form of resistance in itself. “I rap because I want to express myself through my art,” she first tells us. “It’s also because I want other people to be able to identify through my lyrics and my story.”

One of the themes SteinZ portrays with subtlety in her verse is the place of family in young people’s lives – especially young Black people. She speaks of the imperfect relationship between her and her father, and of how a not-insignificant number of young people can identify with her words. “Did you know that single-parent families where the father is absent make up 25% of the Caucasian population? Among Hispanic families, the figure rises to 50%. Among Black families, it’s around 70%,”*** she tells us.
Pour SteinZ, toutes les problématiques f: For SteinZ, all the family issues in these communities are direct historical repercussions of earlier societal problems. “By telling my story through writing my lyrics and rapping them, I’m helping to break this cycle,” she explains.
L’expérience <em>MC Converse</em> a perm: The MC Converse experience allowed SteinZ to continue that process. “Through the workshops, I understood that even if you have a lot of information to get across, you can do it eloquently through rap. My verse in the song is a story I could tell for hours, but I manage it in a few dozen seconds because I learned there’s always a way to share a short story yet touch people for longer,” she concludes.
Si vous vous promenez dans les rues de S: If you stroll the streets of Saint-Michel and stop for a slice of pizza at one of the neighbourhood’s popular pizzerias, chances are you’ll run into a young person with a colourful sense of style and hilarious humour. A public figure across his neighbourhood, DreamKid is a 21-year-old content creator who recently took up the art of rap, to “talk about his neighbourhood and everyday life in Saint-Michel.”

« J’adore apprendre, commence alors Hudl: “I love learning,” begins Hudlain, his real name. “When I saw the chance to learn from Raccoon, one of my favourite local rappers, I jumped at it. Since I’m a ‘part-time rapper,’ I figured it could help me get my lyrics across,” he says with a small half-smile. For him, rap has always been associated with violence, crime, drugs or other vices of life. “The guys I know who rap don’t really talk about love or politics in depth. But rap isn’t just that. You can create stories, tell them with metaphors or other writing techniques,” he continues.
Selon lui, être capable de bien manier c: According to him, being able to handle this art well is a life “skill.” And it’s thanks to that “skill” that he is able to tell his story and that of those around him in his verse over a Kery James instrumental. “Where I’m from is a neighbourhood with a reputation for being a bad place. I want to show people that not everything is black or white, and that there’s a lot of prejudice against my neighbourhood.” He exclaims: “There’s so much to do in Saint-Michel, but nothing gets highlighted. Community organizations don’t have much money, activities get neglected.”
Ce qu’il veut faire, « c’est mettre de l: What he wants to do is “put forward the neighbourhood that watched [him] grow up and avoid prejudices about the place,” he concludes.
Snowside, tout droit sorti du NBS Studio: Snowside, straight out of NBS Studio
Snowside, de son vrai nom Jevonte Junior: Snowside, whose real name is Jevonte Junior, is a 19-year-old who is passionate about rap. “From a very young age, I followed Hip-Hop culture. I spent hours in front of the TV watching Hip-Hop channels in the United States and listening to rappers’ music videos,” begins the Montrealer from Côte-des-Neiges. Asked what motivated him to speak up behind a mic and rap, Snowside says writing has always been a form of escape for him. “Music is like a diary for me,” he explains. “What I write reflects my life, it’s real. I don’t write to please others, I write for myself.”

Et ces paroles, on peut les ressentir ri: And you can feel those words just by reading the lyrics of his verse in Messagers Converse. Snowside talks a lot about the problems of the hood, poverty and precarity, gentrification and the legal troubles that, he says, “almost all racialized youth face.” He goes on in a more optimistic vein: “I wasn’t lucky enough to be born in Hampstead or Westmount into a well-off family. It was hard for me, my path wasn’t strewn with flowers or filled with rainbows. Despite everything, every day I find the beauty to become a better version of myself.”
<em>MC Converse</em> lui a permis de s’e: MC Converse allowed him to express himself through a collective project, recounting the reality of a young person from the neighbourhood with the power of rap. “The rhymes, the patterns, the writing style… It matters when you want to express yourself the right way and move the people listening to you more strongly,” he adds, inspired.
« Je m’exprime pour les autres qui n’ont: “I speak for others who don’t have a voice, or whose voice is harder to hear. That’s my mandate.”
« Si c’est pas pour ma vie, c’est au moi: “If it’s not for my life, it’s at least out of passion that I have to make music,” begins Simone Beaulieu-Cloutier, also known by her stage name Enomis. This passion for writing, at first personal and then necessary for her, pushed her into the world of rap and sung rap. A young Montrealer barely 18 years old, Enomis calls this music her personal “safe space,” which has come to save her on several occasions in her life.

Dans son couplet du morceau produit par: In her verse on the track produced by La Converse, Enomis talks a lot about difference and how it can be used as a strength rather than a weakness by everyone. “You have to be yourself. Everyone makes their own way, but I also notice that a lot of people judge each other at first glance, without even necessarily knowing each other. I wrote this verse because, like it or not, we categorize each other a lot,” she begins. Her desire to comfort young people and encourage them to be honest with themselves and their passions inspired the writing of her verse.
Si les paroles d’Enomis dans la chanson: While Enomis’s lyrics in the song can be perceived differently depending on who is listening, for her it is a very personal matter. “I’ve been recovering from anorexia for two years now. It’s something a lot of young people go through with the arrival of social media, it’s a struggle and a very sensitive subject,” she confides. Having gone through a very difficult process on her road to recovery, the young artist draws on her own experience to raise awareness among those who listen to her and to help prevent the eating disorders that affect the youngest.
« Tout ce qui touche la justice sociale: “Everything that touches on social justice inspires me and motivates me to write songs. I try to be committed, because I think conscious rap in Montréal is necessary,” she concludes.
C’est donc dans l’optique de donner à ce: So it is with the aim of giving these young people from Montréal neighbourhoods the chance to share their concerns that these personalities joined forces – and weaknesses too – in a spirit of teamwork and community. Behind the learning and the completion of this project is also Raccoon.
Artiste déjà à l’aise dans le monde du r: An artist already at home in Montréal’s rap world, he took on the role of mentor to a group of recently emerging young aspiring rappers. So it is through five writing and mentoring workshop sessions, and the organization and creation of La Converse, that the seven apprentice rappers, with little or no experience, had the chance to carry out this project.
<l1>Lui-même étant un « Hood Hero »</l1>: <l1>Himself a “Hood Hero”</l1>, Raccoon understands better than anyone the importance of a project like this. “My goal is to pass on my passion for words and writing to those younger and less experienced than me. Through writing workshops – which I’ve been giving for years in other contexts – I teach everything I’ve learned and mastered since I’ve been immersed in rap,” he explains. He also shares his determination to see a project like this through: “Going all the way and having a concrete result is essential and important. Without that, it’s impossible to see how it can impact the young people taking part in this project.”
En lien avec son rôle de mentor, il esti: Speaking of his role as a mentor, he says what drew him to become an educator was “the concept: taking a conscious rap song and adapting it to the realities of young people in Montréal.” For him, it is also a chance to pass on his passion and his commitment to what he calls “the next generation of Montréal rap.” He also considers La Converse a “good infrastructure for making this idea happen.”
Écrire des lignes de rap engagé, ce n’es: Writing conscious rap lines isn’t just about talking about yourself, but about others too. “One of the foundations of Hip-Hop culture is describing realities and emotions,” says Raccoon. For him, rap and journalism have a lot in common. “It’s important to stick to the facts. And storytelling is a big part of what connects these two worlds!” he continues. Telling a story through facts and emotions can be very informative, no matter the medium used to do it.
<l1>Dans un Montréal où l’on associe enc: In a Montréal where the notion of the hood still carries a pejorative connotation, it is essential to let young people who live in and move through disadvantaged neighbourhoods every day express themselves. Les Messagers Converse rose to the challenge La Converse gave them, through the entire process of writing and learning conscious rap. In their own words, they were able to shed light on the problems and hardships they face, but also on what inspires them every day and what allows them to aspire to change for a better future.
<em>Les Messagers Converse</em> parlent: Les Messagers Converse talk a lot about their own Hood Heroes, but they may not have realized that they are becoming those heroes themselves in the eyes of others.
